cards.front: In genetic engineering, PCR and gel electrophoresis change nothing inside a cell. What are they used for?
cards.back: They test the change. PCR copies one chosen DNA stretch, and a gel sorts DNA pieces by size.
cards.quote: Some tools, such as PCR and gels, change nothing in a cell; they test the change.

cards.front: {{c1::Genetic engineering}} is using laboratory tools to change an organism's DNA.
cards.quote: Genetic engineering is using laboratory tools to change an organism's DNA.
cards.section: Build one change, then test it

cards.front: Why can a bacterium read a human gene that has been put into it, when bacterial control DNA is present?
cards.back: DNA has the same basic structure in living things, and nearly all of them share one genetic code.
cards.why: The gene must also be intron-free for the bacterium to read it.
cards.quote: DNA has the same basic structure in living things, and nearly all of them share one genetic code.
cards.section: Build one change, then test it

cards.front: Why can bacteria generally not read a natural human gene correctly?
cards.back: Most human genes contain introns, which human cells cut out of the RNA message. Bacteria cannot cut them out.
cards.quote: Bacteria cannot cut them out, so they generally cannot read a natural human gene correctly.
cards.section: Build one change, then test it

cards.front: A lab joins a natural human gene, introns included, into a plasmid with the right bacterial control DNA. Will the bacteria read it correctly? What do labs use instead?
cards.back: Generally no, because bacteria cannot cut out introns. Labs use DNA made chemically or copied from the RNA message.
cards.quote: Labs instead use DNA made chemically or copied from the RNA message.
cards.section: Build one change, then test it

cards.front: A {{c1::restriction enzyme}} is a protein from bacteria that cuts DNA wherever it finds one particular short sequence.
cards.quote: A restriction enzyme is a protein from bacteria that cuts DNA wherever it finds one particular short sequence
cards.section: Build one change, then test it

cards.front: A {{c1::plasmid}} is a small, usually circular piece of bacterial DNA that copies separately from the main chromosome.
cards.quote: A plasmid is a small, usually circular piece of bacterial DNA that copies separately from the main chromosome.
cards.section: Build one change, then test it

cards.front: DNA ligase is an enzyme that seals paired ends into one continuous strand, making {{c1::recombinant DNA}}.
cards.back: DNA joined from more than one source.
cards.quote: DNA ligase is an enzyme that seals paired ends into one continuous strand, making recombinant DNA: DNA joined from more than one source.
cards.section: Build one change, then test it

cards.front: In a simple cut-and-join model, a plasmid and a gene are cut with enzymes that leave ends that do not match. Will adding ligase make the intended recombinant plasmid?
cards.back: No. The mismatched ends do not pair, so ligase has nothing to seal. This is why the same enzyme is often used on both.
cards.why: Some real pairs of different enzymes do leave pairable ends, but the first model keeps to matching ends.
cards.quote: Some real pairs of different enzymes do leave ends that can pair, but this first model keeps to matching ends.
cards.section: Build one change, then test it

cards.front: Why does each step of cutting, joining and copying DNA work on only some molecules or cells?
cards.back: The tools are molecules acting by chance in a tube, so each step reaches only some molecules or cells.
cards.quote: they are molecules acting by chance in a tube, so each step works on only some molecules or cells.
cards.section: Build one change, then test it

cards.front: Growing bacteria with an antibiotic so that mostly those carrying a plasmid with a resistance gene survive is called {{c1::selection}}.
cards.quote: so growing the bacteria with that antibiotic, called selection, leaves mostly the ones that took up a plasmid.
cards.section: Build one change, then test it

cards.front: The {{c1::polymerase chain reaction (PCR)}} uses primers and a DNA-copying enzyme to make many copies of one chosen DNA stretch.
cards.back: Primers mark where copying starts.
cards.quote: The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) uses short DNA pieces called primers, which mark where copying starts
cards.section: Build one change, then test it

cards.front: In the ideal PCR model, a tube starts with 4 copies of the target. How many copies after 5 cycles?
cards.back: The amount doubles each cycle: 4 × 2^5 = 4 × 32 = 128 copies.
cards.why: Real reactions copy a bit less than perfectly.
cards.quote: In the ideal model, the amount doubles each cycle.
cards.section: Build one change, then test it

cards.front: {{c1::Gel electrophoresis}} sorts DNA pieces by size.
cards.quote: Gel electrophoresis sorts DNA pieces by size.
cards.section: Build one change, then test it

cards.front: In gel electrophoresis, why does DNA move toward the positive end of the gel?
cards.back: DNA has a negative electric charge, so the current pulls it toward the positive end.
cards.quote: DNA has a negative electric charge, so current pulls it toward the positive end of a gel.
cards.section: Build one change, then test it

cards.front: A gel ladder has bands at 500 and 1,000 base pairs. Where should a piece about 300 base pairs long stop?
cards.back: Farther along the gel than the 500 base-pair band, because shorter pieces travel farther.
cards.quote: Shorter pieces slip through the gel faster and travel farther.
cards.section: Build one change, then test it

cards.front: A band on a gel lines up with the expected size on a ladder. What does that show, and what does it not show?
cards.back: It estimates the piece's size. It does not show the DNA sequence, so sequencing would confirm it is the intended DNA.
cards.quote: Comparing a band with a ladder of known sizes estimates the piece's size, but not its DNA sequence.
cards.section: Build one change, then test it

cards.front: In a common version of CRISPR, what do the guide RNA and Cas9 each do?
cards.back: The guide RNA helps aim Cas9 at a matching DNA region. Cas9 cuts both strands, and the cell then repairs the cut.
cards.quote: In a common version, a guide RNA helps aim Cas9 at a matching DNA region, and Cas9 cuts both strands.
cards.section: From one product to many uses

cards.front: Why must the final result of a CRISPR edit be tested?
cards.back: Unintended sites may also be changed.
cards.quote: The final change must be tested, because unintended sites may also be changed.
cards.section: From one product to many uses

cards.front: Why is Casgevy not called a genetically modified organism, even though it changes DNA?
cards.back: It modifies a patient's cells outside the body, not a whole organism.
cards.quote: Casgevy is different: it modifies a patient's cells outside the body, not a whole organism.
cards.section: From one product to many uses

cards.front: A post claims CRISPR can change every trait in an adult overnight. Using Casgevy as the case, how do you test this claim?
cards.back: The claim fails. Only one kind of cell is edited and returned after chemotherapy, doctors follow results for months, and sperm, eggs and skin are not edited.
cards.why: Rule: judge a claim against what the actual treatment does.
cards.quote: Only one kind of cell is edited and returned after chemotherapy, and doctors follow results for months.
cards.section: From one product to many uses

cards.front: In the USDA survey, soybeans with engineered varieties were 85 percent of U.S. planted acres in 2004 and 96 percent in 2024. What was the change?
cards.back: 96 - 85 = 11 percentage points.
cards.quote: Each June, USDA asks farmers what they planted.
cards.section: Elaborate: how common are engineered crops?

cards.front: In the USDA survey table, soybeans were 54, 85 and 92 percent engineered in 2000, 2004 and 2008. Corn was 25, 47, 80, 86 and 92 in 2000, 2004, 2008, 2010 and 2016. Which crop first reached 90 percent, and in which year shown?
cards.back: Soybeans, in 2008 (92 percent). Corn first reached 90 percent in 2016 (92 percent).
cards.quote: Which crop reached 90 percent first, and in which year shown?
cards.section: Elaborate: how common are engineered crops?

cards.front: A student uses the USDA national table of engineered crop acres to describe farms in Virginia. What is wrong with this?
cards.back: The table gives national estimates, and Virginia is not listed separately. Virginia-specific data would be needed.
cards.quote: These are national estimates. What would you need before using them to describe Virginia farms?
cards.section: Elaborate: how common are engineered crops?

cards.front: In an experiment to show bacteria are making insulin from a plasmid, why include bacteria given the same plasmid with no insulin DNA?
cards.back: It is the control. If it gives no insulin signal while the insulin group does, the signal points to the added DNA.
cards.quote: bacteria given the same plasmid with no insulin DNA (the control)
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In the insulin plasmid experiment, bacteria given no DNA are grown on antibiotic plates. What should happen, and what does it show?
cards.back: They should not grow, which shows the antibiotic works. On a plate without antibiotic they should grow, showing the cells were alive.
cards.quote: Bacteria given nothing should not grow, showing the antibiotic works.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In the insulin plasmid experiment, what antibody-test result do you expect from the empty-plasmid group and from the insulin-plasmid group, and why?
cards.back: The empty-plasmid group should give no signal. The insulin group should give a signal, which points to the added DNA.
cards.quote: The empty-plasmid group should give no signal, so a signal in the insulin group points to the added DNA.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A gel of plasmid cut from a colony shows a backbone band plus an insert-sized band, but the antibody test for insulin gives no signal. What can you conclude?
cards.back: The DNA check passed, but the product check did not show insulin. The two tests answer different questions: the gel checks the DNA, the antibody test checks the product.
cards.why: Rule: a signal shows insulin is present; the gel shows only DNA.
cards.quote: Check the product: test each group for insulin with an antibody test.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A web page says a new engineered seed is safe and everyone should buy it. Which questions about the source and the claim should you ask?
cards.back: Who wrote it, what evidence is given, and was it checked by other scientists? Also, does the writer gain from your belief? Then judge this product on its own benefits, risks and ethics.
cards.quote: add one more: does the writer gain from your belief?
cards.section: From one product to many uses
